background.definition: Tardive dyskinesia (TD) is a disabling, disfiguring movement disorder, involving involuntary choreoathetoid movements of the orofacial region caused primarily by the prolonged use of neuroleptic drugs. It is typically persistent with no definitive treatment.

list.listitem: 3.9% per year for second-generation antipsychotics and 5.5% for first-generation antipsychotics in all patients receiving chronic treatment.
In adults, the annual rate of development with second-generation antipsychotics is 2.98% versus 7.7% with first-generation antipsychotics.
In children, the annual TD incidence rate is 0.35% with second-generation antipsychotics.
Prevalence rates were 13.1% for second-generation antipsychotics, 15.6% for antipsychotic-free patients, and 32.4% for first-generation antipsychotics (P <.0001).
Across 41 studies (n = 11,493), the mean prevalence was 25.3%, with lower prevalence for patients using second-generation rather than first-generation antipsychotics.
TD is caused by prolonged exposure to neuroleptic drugs and is a function of dose and duration.
Atypical antipsychotics appear to have a decreased likelihood of causing TD, but this may be related to dose.
The pathophysiology is not well understood but has as its basis chronic blockade of dopamine in the CNS.
This blockade may lead to supersensitivity or upregulation of dopamine receptors or an imbalance in effect between D1 and D2 receptors.
May have component of central cholinergic deficiency.
Adenosine may play a role.
Evaluate for TD yearly using the in patients receiving neuroleptic treatment. C
If abnormal movements are present, try to decrease neuroleptic dose or switch to atypical if using typical neuroleptic. C
Avoid neuroleptics whenever possible. If necessary, use the minimum neuroleptic dose required to control symptoms. C
Do not use neuroleptics for treatment of behavior. C
Evaluate involuntary, abnormal movements of the face or extremities in patients taking neuroleptics or discontinuing neuroleptics within the past 4 weeks. C

Differential.Differential_Features: No use of neuroleptics; associated with intellectual decline

list.listitem: History is best obtained and documented by using the (see ).
Facial movements include frowning, blinking, grimacing, lip pouting, puckering, or smacking, biting, chewing, lateral movements of the jaw, and increased tongue movement.
Extremity movement can be either rapid, spasmodic, and purposeless or slow, irregular, and serpentine (but not tremor).
Body: rocking, twisting, pelvic gyrations, and diaphragm movements.
General: feeling of restlessness (tardive akathesia).
Movements can be temporarily suppressed by using the affected area, for example, opening the mouth will stop the facial movements.
No specific laboratory or imaging studies exist for this condition.
Carefully monitor patients taking neuroleptics for symptoms of TD. C
History or direct observation will establish the diagnosis in patients taking neuroleptic drugs.
Discontinuing neuroleptic may decrease symptoms, although not in all patients. B
Based on limited research, lowering the dose or switching to another neuroleptic does not decrease TD symptoms. B
Vitamin E may prevent worsening of TD, but no data exist to support vitamin E as an effective treatment. B

The VMAT2 inhibitor deutetrabenazine is approved for the treatment of TD in adults, at a starting dose of 6 mg bid increased weekly to a maximum dose of 24 mg bid. The NNT = 5 for comparison with placebo as defined as much or very much improved.
B
Prevention and prompt recognition of signs and symptoms are key. Stopping the neuroleptic drug or decreasing the dose may reverse the symptoms, although not in all patients.

Based on limited research, lowering the dose or switching to another neuroleptic does not decrease TD symptoms. However, in an uncontrolled trial, olanzapine was effective in decreasing symptoms in patients with persistent TD.

Deutetrabenazine is a vascular monoamine transporter 2 (VMAT2) inhibitor and is approved for the treatment of TD in adults, at a starting dose of 6 mg bid increased weekly to a maximum dose of 24 mg bid. The NNT = 5 for comparison with placebo as deined as much or very much improved. The drug carries a black box warning for depression and suicidality in patients with Huntington's disease.
A systematic review identified 4 clinical trials comparing the VMAT2 inhibitors deutetrabenazine and valbenazine with placebo for the treatment of TD. Both drugs were found to be effective.
A systematic review found 16 clinical trials of clozapine for treatment of TD. They found a significant benefit, especially for patients with more severe TD.
A systematic review found a small effect size for reduction in symptoms with vitamin E.
Preliminary research suggests that benzodiazepines may improve symptoms, although the evidence is not strong enough to support routine use.

Gabapentin, calcium channel blockers, choline, physostigmine, baclofen, progabide, sodium valproate, ceruletide, gamma-linolenic acid, estrogen, lithium and calcium channel blockers have not been shown to be effective.
Vitamin E may prevent worsening of TD, but there is no research confirming vitamin E as an effective treatment.
TD is often irreversible. C
The prognosis is worse for patients who have been on neuroleptics for a longer length of time. B
Increased risk exists for TD in older patients.
Relatively low 1-year rates are seen in pediatric patients treated with second-generation antipsychotics, but low doses were used. Better data exist for risperidone; others had smaller sample sizes.
Risk may be higher in children and adolescents treated with higher doses of second-generation antipsychotics and for a longer period of time.

feature.caption: Abnormal Involuntary Movement Scale (AIMS).
feature.feature_body:
• Scoring: Items are scored on a 0 (none) to 4 (severe) basis; the scale provides a total score (items 1 through 7) or item 8 can be used in isolation as an indication of overall severity of symptoms.
• Instruction: There are 2 parallel procedures, the examination procedure, which tells the patient what to do, and the scoring procedure, which tells the clinician how to rate what he or she observes.
• Examination Procedure: Either before or after completing the examination procedure, observe the patient unobtrusively at rest (eg, in the waiting room). The chair to be used in this examination should be a hard, firm one without arms.
1 Ask the patient whether there is anything in his or her mouth (such as gum or candy) and, if so, to remove it.
2 Ask about the "current" condition of the patient's teeth. Ask if he or she wears dentures. Ask whether teeth or dentures bother the patient "now."
3 Ask whether the patient notices any movements in his or her mouth, face, hands, or feet. If yes, ask the patient to describe them and to indicate to what extent they "currently" bother the patient or interfere with activities.
4 Have the patient sit in the chair with hands on knees, legs slightly apart, and feet flat on floor. (Look at the entire body for movements while the patient is in this position.)
5 Ask the patient to sit with hands hanging unsupported—if male, between his legs, if female and wearing a dress, hanging over her knees. (Observe hands and other body areas.)
6 Ask the patient to open his or her mouth. (Observe the tongue at rest within the mouth.) Do this twice.
7 Ask the patient to protrude his or her tongue. (Observe abnormalities of tongue movement.) Do this twice.
8 Ask the patient to tap his or her thumb with each finger as rapidly as possible for 10 to 15 seconds, first with right hand, then with left hand. (Observe facial and leg movements.) [± activated]
9 Flex and extend the patient's left and right arms, one at a time.
10 Ask the patient to stand up. (Observe the patient in profile. Observe all body areas again, hips included.)
11 Ask the patient to extend both arms out in front, palms down. (Observe trunk, legs, and mouth.) [activated]
12 Have the patient walk a few paces, turn, and walk back to the chair. (Observe hands and gait.) Do this twice. [activated]
Scoring Procedure: Complete the examination procedure before making ratings. For the movement ratings (the first 3 categories below), rate the highest severity observed, 0 = none, 1 = minimal (may be extreme normal), 2 = mild, 3 = moderate, and 4 = severe. According to the original AIMS instructions, one point is subtracted if movements are seen only on activation, but not all investigators follow that convention.
• Facial and Oral Movements:
1 Muscles of facial expression, for example, movements of forehead, eyebrows, periorbital area, cheeks. Include frowning, blinking, grimacing of upper face. 0 1 2 3 4
2 Lips and perioral area, for example, puckering, pouting, smacking. 0 1 2 3 4
3 Jaw, for example, biting, clenching, chewing, mouth opening, lateral movement. 0 1 2 3 4
4 Tongue: Rate only increase in movement both in and out of mouth, not inability to sustain movement. 0 1 2 3 4
• Extremity Movements:
1 Upper (arms, wrists, hands, and fingers): Include movements that are choreic (rapid, objectively purposeless, irregular, and spontaneous) or athetoid (slow, irregular, complex, and serpentine). Do not include tremor (repetitive, regular, and rhythmic movements). 0 1 2 3 4
2 Lower (legs, knees, ankles, and toes), for example, lateral knee movement, foot tapping, heel dropping, foot squirming, inversion and eversion of foot. 0 1 2 3 4
• Trunk Movements:
1 Neck, shoulders, hips, for example, rocking, twisting, squirming, pelvic gyrations. Include diaphragmatic movements. 0 1 2 3 4
• Global Judgments:
1 Severity of abnormal movements. 0 1 2 3 4 based on the highest single score on the above items.
2 Incapacitation due to abnormal movements. 0 = none, normal 1 = minimal, 2 = mild, 3 = moderate, 4 = severe.
3 Patient's awareness of abnormal movements. 0 = no awareness, 1 = aware, no distress, 2 = aware, mild distress, 3 = aware, moderate distress, 4 = aware, severe distress.
• Dental Status:
1 Current problems with teeth and/or dentures. 0 = no, 1 = yes.
2 Does patient usually wear dentures? 0 = no, 1 = yes.
